summary: Fine-tuning makes sense when you need to consistently change a model's behavior, style, or output format, teach it a narrow domain vocabulary, or improve reliability on a repeatable task where prompt engineering has plateaued. RAG is the better choice when you need the model to access up-to-date or proprietary knowledge that changes frequently, while prompt engineering should always be exhausted first because it is the cheapest and fastest to iterate. In practice, many production systems combine a lightly fine-tuned model (for format/behavior) with RAG (for knowledge) rather than choosing one exclusively.
when_to_fine_tune: Choose fine-tuning when you have a high-volume, repeatable task and hundreds-to-thousands of quality examples that encode the exact behavior, tone, or structured output you want.
Choose it when prompt engineering has plateaued and your prompts are becoming long, brittle, or token-expensive just to enforce consistent behavior.
Prefer RAG instead when the core need is factual, proprietary, or frequently-changing knowledge rather than changing the model's inherent behavior or style.
Avoid fine-tuning for fast-moving information or when you lack a clean, representative labeled dataset, since a poorly-curated dataset will degrade rather than improve performance.
